cover.headline: A decades-old unsolved problem in combinatorics may have **a practical solution** that runs in polynomial time.

slides.title: Marton's conjecture deals with sets that grow slowly when you add them to themselves.
slides.body:
When you take a set of numbers and add each element to every other element, you get a new set. How much bigger can it get? If it stays relatively small, the original set must have hidden structure.

A conjecture from the 1990s predicted that any such set can be efficiently covered by shifted copies of a subspace. The theoretical proof arrived in 2025, but it offered no way to actually find that subspace.

slides.title: The team reports an algorithm that finds the covering subspace in polynomial time.
slides.body:
Given a set with doubling constant at most K, their algorithm outputs a subspace no larger than the original set. That subspace, when shifted in at most K to a polynomial power different ways, covers the entire original set.

The algorithm runs in polynomial time with respect to both the dimension n and the doubling constant K. It works by sampling from the set and querying membership, not by examining every element.

slides.title: The algorithmic version unlocks polynomial-time solutions to several learning problems in quantum computing.
slides.body:
The authors apply their result to problems that previously lacked efficient algorithms. These include quadratic Goldreich-Levin, a cryptographic primitive, and two quantum state tomography tasks involving stabilizer states.

Each application relies on the ability to efficiently find structure in sets with bounded growth. The preprint demonstrates that a long-standing theoretical conjecture can yield computational tools, not just existence proofs.

caveats: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has verified the work yet.
The abstract does not specify whether the algorithm has been tested on real-world data or remains a theoretical construction.
The applications to quantum tomography depend on assumptions about oracle access that may not hold in all experimental settings.

cta.headline: Send this to the polynomial time skeptic
cta.sub: One real study, every weekday. The full paper is linked in bio.

caption: Marton's polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture, first posed in the 1990s, predicts that sets with bounded doubling must have hidden algebraic structure. A team working on the heels of a 2025 theoretical proof now reports an algorithm that actually finds that structure in polynomial time. The algorithm takes a set in n-dimensional binary space with doubling constant at most K and outputs a subspace of comparable size whose polynomial number of translates cover the original set. The team demonstrates applications to quadratic Goldreich-Levin and two quantum state tomography problems. Published as a preprint on arXiv with no experimental validation reported. The method has not yet been peer reviewed. Full study: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20771v1 — Send this to the person in your life who insists pure math never produces practical algorithms.

The abstract does not state when Marton's conjecture was posed. The '1990s' timeframe is not mentioned in the abstract.

The abstract says 'Annals '25' which likely refers to a journal publication year, but this could also be interpreted as a volume number or other designation. The copy definitively states it as the year 2025, which is not explicitly stated in the abstract.
